name: Rafael Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grow apples and pears at Ashby Orchards, forty hectares, which my family has farmed for four generations. Cox and Bramleys mostly, Bramleys are the big sour cooking apples, and a block of Conference pears. In November the picking's done and the fruit's in cold store, so I'm walking the rows with my secateurs starting the winter pruning. It's slow, quiet work. Every cut decides what that tree gives you in two years' time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pruning, honestly, more than picking. You stand in front of a tree your grandfather planted and you have a conversation with it. What wears me out is the selling. The wholesaler pays what he likes, and half my Bramleys go to the cider works at a price that barely covers the picking.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My foreman, George Pruitt, has been here twenty-six years. At picking time I take on about twenty-five people, a lot of them local families, mothers whose kids are at school, and some men who come back every year. My wife Margaret does the books by hand and runs the choir at St Michael's, where I'm a churchwarden.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology or AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not if I can help it. We've got a cold store with a computer controller, because the insurance demanded it. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't intend to. My son-in-law keeps showing me things on his phone and I keep saying, that's nice, son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a tool, and tools are fine in their place. I'd also say people put too much faith in gadgets and not enough in hard work. At church coffee after the service I'd say the same thing, and most would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me, and I'm glad. My trouble is the prices, and the rules from people in offices who've never pruned a tree. A search engine won't fix either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd replant two rows of old Cox that are past their best, about three thousand in trees and stakes, and they won't fruit properly for four years. I'd keep George and the picking crew as they are. I'd keep doing the books on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Satisfied, really, that the fuss was about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Planting trees that take four years. How do you think about that at fifty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandfather planted these trees for a grandson he never met. You don't do that with a machine that's out of date in three years. You plant for whoever comes next. If I only planted for myself, I'd have stopped years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rules from people in offices. Which rules?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pesticide forms, the water forms, the labour forms. Every year there's a new one. Margaret spends a week every spring on paperwork for a government that doesn't seem to want us to grow fruit at all. I'm not against rules. I'm against rules written by people who've never had frost in May.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a tool and tools are fine in their place, but people put too much faith in gadgets and not enough in hard work.
S0.think: Privately it changes nothing for me and I'm glad. My real trouble is prices and office rules written by people who've never pruned a tree.
S0.do: Replants two rows of old Cox trees for about three thousand, knowing they won't fruit for four years. Keeps George, the picking crew and the paper books as they are.
S0.feel: Calm and satisfied that the fuss was about nothing.
S0.quote: My grandfather planted these trees for a grandson he never met. You don't do that with a machine that's out of date in three years.
S0.fieldNote: He thinks in decades, through trees, and frames everything through family and duty. His grievance is with office rules more than with technology. Firm but not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is how it should be, give people time and keep them working. And if companies stop taking on youngsters, that's a moral failing. A young man needs work to learn who he is. I'd say that at church, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow suits me fine. I'll be done before it gets here. But the lads in the village, some of them pick for me in the summer, and if there are no starter jobs in town, they'll drift. I've seen what happens to young men with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on an apprentice, a local lad, and George would teach him pruning and grafting properly, the way he taught me. The college has a fruit-growing apprenticeship, and the government covers part of the wage. I'd pay the rest, about eight thousand a year from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about myself. A bit troubled for the young lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've seen what happens to young men with nothing to do. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret's nephew, Danny. Left school, couldn't get a job, spent two years in his bedroom on his computer. It took his uncle getting him on a building site to bring him back to life. Work isn't just money. It gives you somewhere to be at seven in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should help, or is it up to families?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, and the church, and employers like me. The government can help with the apprenticeships, I'll take that. But handouts don't make a man. A trade does.

S1.say: I'd say slow is how it should be, and companies not hiring youngsters is a moral failing. A young man needs work to learn who he is.
S1.think: Privately slow suits me, since I'll be done before it arrives. I worry about village lads who pick for me and would drift with no starter jobs in town.
S1.do: Takes on a local apprentice through the college fruit-growing scheme, paying about eight thousand a year on top of the government share. Has George teach him pruning and grafting.
S1.feel: Calm about himself, troubled for the young lads.
S1.quote: Work isn't just money. It gives you somewhere to be at seven in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: His concern for young men is moral as much as economic, and the Danny story is personal. He accepts government help for apprenticeships but draws a clear line at handouts. Consistent with his traditional views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it serves some of them right, the people in offices who made our lives harder with forms. No, that's unkind. I'd say it's a hard thing and people should look after their own families and churches first, and not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think, good, maybe the forms get simpler. But Margaret's sister works in a solicitor's office, and our daughter Ruth does admin for the county council. That's two in the family, and I'd be worried for them, much more than I'd let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth that if things went badly, she and the children could move into the old farm cottage, rent free. I'd hold off on replanting the Cox rows that year. And I'd ask George whether Ruth could help in the packing shed at picking time, if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Ruth and the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You started by saying it served them right. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's the bit of me that's been filling in pesticide forms for thirty years. When it's Ruth, it's different. She's not the one who wrote the forms. She types up planning letters for a living. She's a good girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruth actually come and work in the packing shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it. She hasn't packed apples since she was sixteen. But she'd do it, because she's my daughter and she doesn't sit about. That's how we raised her. I'd be proud and sad at the same time.

S2.say: I'd say it's a hard thing and people should look after their own families and churches first, not wait for the government.
S2.think: Privately I'd hope the forms get simpler, but I'd worry about my daughter Ruth doing council admin and my sister-in-law at a solicitor's office.
S2.do: Offers Ruth and the grandchildren the old farm cottage rent free if things go badly. Delays replanting the Cox rows and asks George about work for Ruth in the packing shed.
S2.feel: Uneasy, mostly for Ruth and the grandchildren.
S2.quote: No. That's the bit of me that's been filling in pesticide forms for thirty years. When it's Ruth, it's different.
S2.fieldNote: He catches his own unkind first reaction and corrects it when it touches family. His answer to the crisis is family and property, not policy. The packing shed plan shows his faith in work as dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to keep calm and stop demanding the government hand out other people's money. If share prices are up, good for the people who saved. But I'd also say the men who built these machines owe the country something, and they should pay their taxes like the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about the village. If house prices boom, my pickers can't afford to live here. The mothers who pick for me rent in the village, and if landlords sell to city people, they're gone. I can't pick forty hectares with George and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do up the two old farm cottages for pickers' families, rent cheap, so I keep my crew. That's maybe sixty thousand, so I'd borrow against the land. I'd also talk to the vicar about the church helping families who've lost work, with food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The trees will be fine, but I need hands to pick them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd borrow sixty thousand against the land. That's a big step for someone who avoids risk.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I've never borrowed against the land. My father would turn in his grave. But a cottage is a brick thing you can stand in, not a share price. If I keep my pickers, I keep the orchard. If I lose them, the land's worth nothing to me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the men who built the machines should pay their taxes. Isn't that what the other side is asking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm not for handouts, I'm for fairness. If you make a fortune from something that throws ten thousand people out of work, you don't get to fly off to an island. That's not left or right. That's just decent.

S3.say: I'd say people should stop demanding the government hand out other people's money. But the men who built these machines owe the country something and should pay their taxes.
S3.think: Privately I worry that a house price boom will push my pickers out of the village. Without the mothers who rent locally and pick for me, I can't harvest forty hectares.
S3.do: Borrows about sixty thousand against the land, for the first time, to do up two farm cottages as cheap homes for pickers' families. Asks the vicar about church help with food and school costs.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the trees will be fine but he needs hands to pick them.
S3.quote: If you make a fortune from something that throws ten thousand people out of work, you don't get to fly off to an island.
S3.fieldNote: When gently pointed out that his tax line matches the other side, he redefines it as decency, not politics. His willingness to borrow against the land, a first, shows how serious the threat to his crew feels. Housing again matters more than the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, plain wrong. Robots in care homes and on farms, taking away the work that gives people their dignity. I'd say it from the church steps if I had to. And I'd say I'll never buy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm frightened. They're already testing robots that pick apples with suction tubes, I've seen it in the farming paper. If the big orchards get them, their fruit will be cheaper, and the wholesaler will pay me robot prices for hand-picked apples. I can't win that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy one, not in the first year, maybe not ever. I'd try to sell direct, a stall in town, a pick-your-own weekend, a deal with the farm shop up the road, so I'm less tied to the wholesaler. I'd keep George to the end. And I'd start talking to Ruth's husband about whether he wants the land, because I won't be the one to bring the robots in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And grieving, a bit, for the way things were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the picking crew, if you couldn't keep them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them myself, in the barn, at the end of the season. Not a letter. Some of those mothers have picked for me for fifteen years. I'd give them each a bonus, and a box of Bramleys, and I'd say I'm sorry. I'd probably say it badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never buy one, but you'd hand the land to your son-in-law. Would he buy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. He's the sort. I suppose that means I'm passing the decision on rather than making it. Margaret would say I'm being a coward. Maybe. But I'd rather the trees go on with robots than be dug up for houses.

S4.say: I'd say robots taking work that gives people dignity is plain wrong, and I'd say it from the church steps. I'd also say I'll never buy one.
S4.think: Privately I'm frightened, because apple-picking robots already exist. If big orchards use them, the wholesaler will pay me robot prices for hand-picked apples and I can't win that.
S4.do: Refuses to buy a robot and tries selling direct through a town stall, pick-your-own weekends and a nearby farm shop. Keeps George to the end and talks to his son-in-law about taking over the land.
S4.feel: Alarmed and grieving for the way things were.
S4.quote: But I'd rather the trees go on with robots than be dug up for houses.
S4.fieldNote: His public anger is moral and religious, and his private fear is about price. He admits he's passing the robot decision to his son-in-law rather than making it. The final choice, trees with robots over houses, shows his deepest loyalty is to the orchard itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, without a doubt. The others hurt my family, but the robots take the thing I know how to do and make it worthless. What would help is honest labelling, so people can choose fruit picked by people, and the wholesalers made to pay a fair price. Not handouts. Just a fair chance for small growers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I don't know how to say it without sounding like a sermon. But a lot of people round here will get through this because of their church, their neighbours, their families. Not because of an app. Somebody should write that down.

headlineQuote: My grandfather planted these trees for a grandson he never met. You don't do that with a machine that's out of date in three years.
portrait: Rafael Young is fifty-eight and grows apples and pears on forty hectares at Ashby Orchards, farmed by his family for four generations, with his foreman George and a crew of local pickers. He's a churchwarden with traditional views who distrusts gadgets and handouts but believes deeply in work as dignity. The office pictures reach him through his daughter Ruth, and the fast picture through housing for his pickers, which drives him to borrow against the land for the first time. Faced with robots, he refuses to buy one himself but admits he'd rather the orchard go on with robots under his son-in-law than be lost.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because robots would make the skill he knows worthless and leave him unable to compete on price.
whatWouldHelp: Honest labelling so people can choose fruit picked by people, and wholesalers made to pay small growers a fair price.
